Please view the project papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/, and specifically look at research-overview/02_PAIR_SPECTRUM_CURVED_CONTOURS_AND_CONDITIONAL_SIMPLICITY_PROGRAM_20261023.md and the corresponding progress file 02_PAIR_SPECTRUM_AND_CURVED_CONTOUR_PROGRESS_20261023. 

We are systematically investigating the different routes within this program. Please begin the research, record your research within the notes folders, update progress in the progress file, and chat histories within the chat-histories folder. Continue until all tasks are finished or you run out of compute budget.
I’ll read the program, progress record, and repository guidance, then investigate independent routes in parallel and save the results, progress updates, and chat history in the project.

The existing program gives finite implications from a spectral bound to simplicity, but the required theta-source bound is still open. I’m working on that source estimate while parallel investigations address contour transport, backward stability, and the passage to growing height. This chat is registered as history 0002.

Two useful estimates are taking shape: a sharper finite bound on repeated endpoint labels, and a bound on how distant zeros affect the filtered spectrum. The latter stays finite when internal gaps shrink. The contour and backward work is also identifying the wall accuracy and terminal precision needed before those methods can give a simplicity result.

The source calculation now gives an explicit bound: distant zeros contribute at most a constant times \(N\log R/R\) to the filter derivative, uniformly as internal gaps shrink. The nearby coupled contribution still needs control. I’m checking the new arguments and screening the available late-time estimates against the microscopic scale required by the program.

One route now has a clearer limitation: in the range where the published high-height clock theorem applies, the normalized filter tends to its maximum, not to zero. That rules out using that theorem directly for the proposed upper bound. The separate backward calculation also shows why independently bounding its late-time errors loses too much precision; correlated source estimates remain open.

The four notes, reviews, progress updates, and replay records are saved; all checks pass. I’m pursuing one further finite question: whether the contour method can enclose the spectral filter directly from polynomial coefficients, avoiding separate isolation of every root. That could make the source-to-filter step more usable near a collision.

The follow-up has a useful finite result: a polynomial formula can enclose the filter without isolating each root, including near a double collision. Higher collisions need more care. The analysis identifies the source accuracy required after rescaling at heat time \(t\), rather than treating division by a vanishing discriminant as harmless.

The coefficient method now has a precise scope: at a fixed positive filter scale it stays regular through separated double collisions, including simultaneous doubles. Triple collisions require additional normalization or a justified real-root restriction. I’m checking those distinctions against the exact examples before adding the result to the progress record.

The checks passed. The main finite improvements are the sharper bound \(M_0\le4q\) and a way to enclose \(q\) from polynomial coefficients without separating every root. The late-time analysis also identifies two approaches that do not close the required estimate. I’m saving these results while keeping the missing microscopic theta bound explicitly open.

The new coefficient formula suggests one further route worth testing: transport the whole prepared polynomial backward, then evaluate the filter from its coefficients. I’ll check whether this preserves cancellations lost by separate root-error bounds, and derive the error cost from the exterior force explicitly.

The polynomial calculation gives a useful distinction. Backward transport of the heat term alone has an explicit polynomial error factor at fixed degree. Including the full theta force requires a separate bound, but that bound can use values on an enclosing wall and remain finite through internal collisions. It still needs accurate source data on that wall.

The closed coefficient equation has a stronger structure than expected: its matrices commute and lower polynomial degree. Its exact backward propagator is therefore a finite polynomial in integrated wall moments. I’m checking the resulting error bound and its dependence on degree and moment size; those quantities can still be large.

The remaining cost is now explicit in this approach: integrated wall moments require a certified lower bound for the full theta field on the wall, together with derivative or analytic-neighborhood error bounds. The finite propagator does not depend on internal root separation, but its cost can grow with the population size and the acquired moment bounds.

The coefficient transport checks passed on examples with nonzero exterior force and on a stationary sine control. The latter catches an important error: dropping the exterior force predicts motion where the roots are stationary. The note now keeps that force and distinguishes the full-source error bound from the unforced heat bound.

Review found two presentation issues: the two-root comparison needed an explicit fixed-center assumption, and one wall formula had a formatting error. The finite transport theorem passed the mathematical review. I’m incorporating the corrections and finalizing the notes, checks, progress record and chat archive.

The research is saved through Note 12. The checks now total 1,333 exact rational assertions, and the link, formula-delimiter and file-size checks pass. The progress record separates the finite theorems from the remaining source problem: acquiring a theta error budget strong enough to prove the required early-time filter bound.

Saved six research notes (07–12), supporting reviews and checks, and updated the [progress file](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/research-progress/02_PAIR_SPECTRUM_AND_CURVED_CONTOUR_PROGRESS_20261023.md). Chat history was refreshed; final-reply capture is arranged.

Main advances:

- Sharpened the finite multiplicity bound to **\(M_0\le4q\)** under the stated RH-dependent hypotheses.
- Developed coefficient-based filter enclosures and backward transport without internal root-gap denominators.
- Identified precise limitations of two late-time approaches.

**1,333 exact-rational checks passed.**

The program remains unfinished: the crucial microscopic theta upper estimate is still open. No new simplicity theorem is claimed.
The previous turn made substantive progress. I’ll verify the saved state and final chat capture, then focus on acquiring a concrete theta estimate for the new coefficient method.

The repository already has an Arb-based evaluator for the complete time-zero theta field. A short heat-time expansion appears sufficient for the prescribed finite box: its remainder can be bounded from the positive theta source. I’ll use this as a bounded test of the acquisition method; it would not establish a global simplicity result.

The first complete theta certificate has succeeded on the prescribed finite box. It certifies two distinct zeros throughout the full complex time window, with a positive boundary margin, without assuming isolated root locations. I’m checking the calculation independently and recording exactly which parts of the larger program it resolves.

The finite calculation also gives a filter value near \(4.2163\times10^{-6}\), well below the block threshold \(1/2\). This verifies the method on the chosen two-zero box. For the global route, I’m checking a sharper published source approximation; its smaller error comes with an extra analyticity condition that must be paid before contour transport can use it.

The independent audit passed. On this box, direct coefficient evaluation gives a much tighter filter enclosure than the uniform contour-transport bound, so the result does not show a transport advantage. I’m now extending the same complete-source calculation to the original cap and every boundary face, so the comparison includes the spatial complement.
This sounds like some great progress. I think it might be a good time to write up the results into a draft manuscript, and take a step back to brainstorm the best next steps.

I’ll write a working manuscript that separates the proved results, finite theta certificates, and open global estimates. I’ll also save a critical assessment of the next research directions, including what the direct comparisons tell us about where further work is most promising.

I’m using the PDF skill to check the manuscript’s rendered layout. I’ll keep one editable manuscript in the investigation folder, record this milestone in its draft history, and put the next-step assessment in a separate research note.

The bounded cap comparison is now complete: it includes every face and the full spatial complement, but both certified lower bounds are negative. It shows no useful deformation gain at that resolution. I’ll include that limitation in the manuscript alongside the positive results, so the next-step discussion is grounded in both.

The draft is organized around the coefficient transport theorem, the forest-polynomial filter, and the corrected microscopic source reference. The next-step assessments agree: test the corrected full reference on one prescribed high-height block, while recording the wall margin, coefficient error, and final filter bound. More low-height cap refinement is a lower priority unless it tests a specific improvement.

The manuscript compiles as a 19-page draft. Cross-review clarified the scope of the late-time claims, the all-time wall assumptions, and the distinction between coefficient snapshots and actual heat solutions. I’m checking the rendered pages and updating the progress record to match the manuscript and its next-step assessment.

The draft brings together the proofs, finite certificates, and the cap comparison that did not yield a useful bound. I’m finishing the page checks and the next-step assessment, with the remaining global estimate clearly marked as open.

The 19-page draft compiles cleanly, and the rendered pages look sound. The next-step assessment recommends one prescribed high-height test of the corrected reference, compared with a direct calculation using the same information. That should identify the limiting error before a broader campaign.

The previous turn completed the manuscript checkpoint. I’ll now examine the proposed next steps more critically: what each would establish, which assumptions the collision controls defeat, and whether a high-height test would answer a useful new question.
